reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: A non-random co-occurrence of congenital defects; the acronym denotes Vertebral anomalies, Anal atresia, Cardiac defects, Tracheo-oesophageal fistula, Renal anomalies, and Limb (usually radial) defects
Diagnosis is clinical and conventionally requires at least three of the component features in the absence of an alternative unifying syndrome
It is an association rather than a syndrome, meaning the components occur together more often than by chance but without a single known cause
Tracheo-oesophageal fistula with oesophageal atresia often presents in the newborn with choking, drooling, and an inability to pass a feeding tube
Anorectal malformation may be evident at birth as an absent or abnormally placed anus
Limb involvement is typically preaxial or radial, such as a hypoplastic or absent thumb or radius
Intellect is usually normal, and its presence should prompt reconsideration of a specific syndromic diagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: VACTERL association is understood as a pattern of defects affecting structures that develop during a shared early embryonic window, particularly disturbances of blastogenesis and midline mesodermal patterning. The components involve organs derived from or dependent on interactions between mesoderm and endoderm, and disruption of common developmental signalling pathways, including those governing left-right and cranio-caudal patterning, is thought to underlie the clustering. No single genetic cause explains most cases, and it remains a diagnosis of exclusion; recognisable single-gene disorders such as Fanconi anaemia and mitochondrial or ciliary conditions can produce an overlapping phenotype and must be considered before accepting the label.
additionalDifferentials: Fanconi anaemia (radial defects with marrow failure)
additionalInvestigations: Spinal and skeletal radiographs to identify vertebral segmentation and rib anomalies
Echocardiography to characterise congenital heart disease
Contrast or endoscopic evaluation and attempts to pass a nasogastric tube for tracheo-oesophageal fistula
Renal and abdominal ultrasound to detect urinary tract malformation
Limb radiographs to define radial ray defects
Chromosome breakage studies to exclude Fanconi anaemia and targeted genetic testing
redFlags: Neonatal respiratory distress and aspiration from tracheo-oesophageal fistula requiring urgent surgery
High or complex anorectal malformation needing early surgical management
Ductal-dependent or complex cardiac lesion presenting with collapse
Bilateral renal anomalies threatening kidney function
Features suggesting Fanconi anaemia, which carries marrow failure and malignancy risk
reference.prognosis: Prognosis reflects the number and severity of component defects; with modern neonatal surgery and multidisciplinary care many children survive with good function and normal cognition, though cardiac and renal severity are the main determinants of outcome.
pitfalls: Accepting the label without excluding Fanconi anaemia and other definable syndromes
Missing a tracheo-oesophageal fistula in a newborn who chokes with feeds
Failing to complete systematic screening of all component systems once one defect is found
Assuming intellectual disability, which is not typical of the association
Overlooking occult vertebral or renal anomalies that alter management
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Staged surgical correction of individual anomalies, including repair of tracheo-oesophageal fistula and oesophageal atresia, anorectal malformation reconstruction, and cardiac surgery as needed
Neonatal stabilisation with airway protection, prevention of aspiration and safe feeding around the tracheo-oesophageal defect
Correction of radial ray and other limb defects with orthopaedic and hand surgery
Investigation and management of renal and urological anomalies to preserve renal function
Chromosome breakage testing to exclude Fanconi anaemia before accepting the diagnosis
Multidisciplinary coordination across neonatology, paediatric surgery, cardiology, urology, orthopaedics and clinical genetics
Long-term developmental follow-up and family support, with genetic counselling regarding the generally low recurrence risk
